For raw data, Range \(=\) largest value \(-\) smallest value.

Here the largest observation is \(45\) and the smallest is \(7\).

\(\therefore\) Range \(= 45 - 7 = 38\).

Range \(= 38\)

For raw data, Range \(=\) largest value \(-\) smallest value.

The largest observation is \(967\) and the smallest is \(250\).

\(\therefore\) Range \(= 967 - 250 = 717\).

Range \(= 717\)

The variable here is the number of mistakes: \(15, 20, 21, 12, 17, 10\).

Largest \(= 21\) (Wednesday), smallest \(= 10\) (Saturday).

\(\therefore\) Range \(= 21 - 10 = 11\).

Range \(= 11\) mistakes

The variable is the score on the die, not the frequency, so the frequencies play no part in the range.

The scores observed run from \(1\) to \(6\).

\(\therefore\) Range \(= 6 - 1 = 5\).

Range \(= 5\)

For a grouped frequency distribution the range is taken as the difference of the extreme class boundaries, that is

Range \(=\) (upper boundary of the highest class) \(-\) (lower boundary of the lowest class).

The classes are already continuous, so the lowest boundary is \(62\) and the highest is \(72\).

\(\therefore\) Range \(= 72 - 62 = 10\).

Range \(= 10\)
